qt: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI) Subject:

Every year, thousands of workers find themselves in a tight spot due to the shortages of places at nurseries. The Hellenic Agency for Local Development and Local Government (EETAA) granted EUR 158 009 in vouchers for the period 2026-2027, of which EUR 106 133 was for nurseries, while the rest was for state-supported after-school activity centres for children (KDAP). Applications for after-school activity centres and after-school activity centres for children with disabilities were not covered, resulting in 41 129 children being rejected. Existing nurseries are shrinking despite the confirmed shortages of places. The European ‘neighbourhood nannies’ programme is anti-educational and is being used as a substitute for an improved pedagogical approach. In view of this, where does the Commission stand on: 1.

parents’ long-standing call and need for all children to be admitted, without exception and selection criteria, to free and modern nurseries staffed by full-time carers rather than carers on ‘on-demand contracts’ (Directive 2019/1152)?

the fact that, in order to increase the number of women entering the labour market, to secure corporate profit-making, anti-educational care programmes, such as the ‘neighbourhood nannies’ one, are being implemented on the basis of the European Child Guarantee and Recommendation (EU) 2021/1004?

the urgent need for the billions of euros that the EU and national governments are pumping into the war industry and into supporting the profitability of corporate groups to go towards meeting the needs of ordinary people, through the establishment, for instance, of all the much-needed free, modern and upgraded nurseries, fully-staffed with qualified professionals, so that all needs are universally met under updated terms?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.10.2026) The organisation, funding and capacity of nursery systems are primarily matters for the Member States. The EU supports national action through cooperation in education and social policy. Based on Principle 11 of the Pillar of Social Rights, the 2030 Barcelona targets1 encourage access to affordable, inclusive and high-quality early childhood education and care (ECEC). The European Child Guarantee2 also recommends Member States to guarantee a free and effective access for children in need. While both are non-binding instruments and do not prescribe a specific model of ECEC, access and quality are key aspects to foster educational development of children. Greece prepared a national action plan for the Guarantee which it currently implements3. With the help of the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+), the EU supports such implementation. The ESF+ allocation to tackle child poverty and/or to implement the European Child Guarantee in Greece is EUR 682.5 million, representing approximately 12% of the total ESF+ allocation. The total number of children expected to be targeted by the financed measures is more than 288 thousand. Despite important investments, in 2025 the participation rate in ECEC of children below 3 years old at risk of poverty or social exclusion (16.9%) remains more than 10 percentage points below that of children not at risk (29.6%). As part of the Anti-Poverty Strategy, the Commission adopted a Communication on Breaking the cycle of child poverty – strengthening the European Child Guarantee4, which stresses closing such participation gap as a priority. The implementation of the Child Guarantee is also among the four social objectives of the National and Regional Partnership Plans, in the Commission regulation proposal5.
